adults.title: Helping Hands Before Judging Eyes
adults.big_idea: A true disciple of Jesus Christ is quick to help and slow to judge, as the Savior was with the woman at the well.
adults.objective: Learners will name what the Savior did and did not do at the well, and choose one person they will help this week in place of judging.
prepare: Read Elder Sinclair's talk, Quick to Help, Slow to Judge, and John 4:4–42.
Bring paper and pens, or ask learners to use a notes app.
Draw two columns on the board: What the Savior did / What He did not do.
Mark the key quotes below so you can read them aloud or hand them to a reader.

segments.name: Stuck, and someone helped
steps: After the prayer, give everyone one quiet minute to write an answer to the first question below. Tell them no one will have to share details.
Invite learners to turn to a neighbor and share only the second question.
Take one or two answers from the whole class. Say that today's talk is about being that kind of person for someone else.
questions: Think of a time you were stuck in a problem, perhaps one you helped create. Who helped you without first making you feel small?
What did that person's help feel like, and what did it make possible for you?

segments.name: The baffling buttons
steps: Retell Elder Sinclair's story in your own words: during a ward Primary program his young friend James, in a new suit, buttoned his right sleeve to the buttonhole on his left lapel and could not get loose. Elder Sinclair grew more and more aggravated and was shaking his head as James was about to go to the pulpit.
Then tell what happened next: the little girl sitting beside James saw the same thing, wanted to help, and reached up and popped the button out of the buttonhole.

Ask a learner to read the first key quote (T33.06). Explain that Elder Sinclair said he felt relieved but also humbled, and that he quoted Elder Kearon's phrase “a radical reorientation” to describe what his soul needed.
Discuss the questions. Keep it honest and light; Elder Sinclair told this story on himself.
questions: Two people watched the same boy. Why do you think one became irritated and the other moved to help?
Where do you most often find yourself shaking your head when you could be reaching out a hand?

segments.name: At the well
steps: Divide into groups of three or four. Ask each group to read John 4:7–18 and 25–29 and list what the Savior did for the woman and what He chose not to do.
After five minutes, fill in the two columns on the board from the groups' lists.

Read the second and third key quotes (T33.08 and T33.11). Add anything the class missed. Point out that Elder Sinclair said the Savior knew absolutely everything about her and still came to offer living water, and that He responded with teaching, not ridicule.
Read President Chibota's sentence from the aligned quotes and ask the questions below.
questions: Elder Sinclair said we do not know whether she was widowed, divorced or abandoned, and that these are not the details we need. What changes in us when we admit how little we know of another person's story?
The Savior was slow to judge and still trusted her with truth. How did He hold both together?
She came as a pariah and left with a purpose. When has someone looked to your possible and not only your past?

segments.name: Modern-day wells
steps: Explain that Elder Sinclair compared the people missionaries find and teach to men and women at modern-day wells: people who may fear judgment but need help. He prayed that when they meet us they will know they have “come home.”

Read these three generic situations and ask pairs to choose one: a new member arrives late and sits alone at the back; someone returns to church after many years away; a visitor's clothes or manner are not what the ward is used to.
Ask each pair to answer the two questions below in two minutes, then hear from three pairs. Write their helping-hand ideas on the board.
Invite the class to read Matthew 7:1–5 on their own later this week as a private check on their own eyes.
questions: What would judging eyes notice first in this situation?
What would helping hands do in the first five minutes?

segments.name: Reorient and act
steps: Read the invitation from the talk (T33.12) and President Oaks's words that Elder Sinclair quoted: “seek to be holy, like our Savior.”
Read the fourth key quote (T33.13), Elder Sinclair's testimony of what our small and simple help does.
Give two silent minutes. Ask each person to write one name and one small thing they will do for that person this week, and one situation where they will choose to be slower to judge.
Check understanding: ask two volunteers to finish the sentence, A disciple who is quick to help and slow to judge will...
Tell the class that next week you will open by asking what happened when they showed up on someone's ordinary day. Bear your testimony of the Savior, who offers each of us living water.

key_quotes.text: a true disciple of Jesus Christ is quick to help and slow to judge
In her ordinary days, she may have endured many judging eyes but few helping hands—until this day.

He did not hold her hostage to her history. He trusted her with truth. Jesus Christ reminds us that to help people transform their lives, we must look not only to their past—we must look to their possible.
I testify that when we help people, one by one, in our own small and simple ways, rather than judge them, we are preparing the world for the Second Coming of Jesus Christ.

scriptures.use: Read in small groups; list what the Savior did for the woman at the well and what He did not do.
Assign as private reading during the week; learners ask what in their own eye needs attention before they look at another's.
Optional: read the last phrase after the buttons story and ask what the little girl taught the adult who was watching.

aligned_quotes.speaker: President Chibota
aligned_quotes.text: He sees not only who we are but who we can become.

aligned_quotes.speaker: President Dallin H. Oaks
aligned_quotes.text: seek to be holy, like our Savior

invitations.text: we are invited to reorient our souls so we may help friends and new members in more Christlike ways

takeaways: A true disciple of Jesus Christ is quick to help and slow to judge.
The Savior knew everything about the woman at the well and offered her dignity, truth and living water.
Small help given one by one prepares the world for the Savior's return.
act: Choose one friend, new member or returning member and do one small, specific thing for that person before next Sunday.
When you catch yourself shaking your head at someone this week, stop and ask, What help is needed here?
At church next Sunday, sit by or greet someone who is alone before you greet your usual friends.
Read John 4:4–42 at home and pray to see one person's possible.
adapt: At home or with two or three people: skip the groups, read John 4:7–18 aloud together and make the two lists on one sheet of paper.
Large class: let neighbors work in pairs where they sit, and take only three or four reports for the board.
Short on time: tell the buttons story, do the two columns at the well, and go straight to the silent writing.

youth.title: Unbutton, Don't Roll Your Eyes
youth.big_idea: Followers of Jesus Christ are quick to help and slow to judge; the Savior looks at a person's possible, not only at their past.
youth.objective: Youth will find in John 4 how the Savior helped without shaming, and pick one real person to help this week in place of judging.
prepare: Read Elder Sinclair's talk and John 4:4–42.
Ask youth to bring scriptures or have the Gospel Library app ready.
Bring paper and pens, and a timer (a phone works).
Write the four situations from the fourth segment on slips of paper, one per slip.

segments.name: One-arm challenge
steps: As soon as class starts, ask everyone to press their right wrist flat against their left shoulder and keep it there, as if it were buttoned in place.
Start a 45-second timer. With the free hand only, each person must open to John 4, in print or on a phone, and hold it up.
Now allow a neighbor to help anyone who is still struggling. Ask the first question below, then tell them today's talk begins with a boy who got stuck just like this.
questions: When you were stuck, would you rather the person next to you laughed, sighed, or helped?

segments.name: James and the buttons
steps: Tell Elder Sinclair's story: during a ward Primary program, a boy named James buttoned the right sleeve of his new suit jacket to the buttonhole on his left lapel and could not get free. He was pleased, then panicked.
Explain that Elder Sinclair, watching, got more and more aggravated and was shaking his head. The little girl next to James saw the same problem and simply reached up and undid the button.
Read the first two key quotes (T33.05 and T33.06). Ask the questions. Let them answer honestly; Elder Sinclair told all of general conference that his own first reaction was the wrong one.
questions: Be honest: when someone does something awkward or foolish, what is your first reflex?
Why is it sometimes easier to judge than to help?

segments.name: Well race
steps: Form teams of three. Give each team paper. Set a four-minute timer: read John 4:7–15 and 25–29 and write every action of the Savior that helped the woman. Most actions found wins.
Let the winning team read its list. Other teams add anything missed.
Read the third key quote (T33.11) slowly. Ask teams to circle anything on their lists that matches it.

Explain gently what Elder Sinclair pointed out: her life had included broken relationships, and we do not know the reasons. He said those are not the details we need. What the Savior focused on was help.
Ask the questions below.
questions: The Savior knew everything about her. What does it tell you that He started with a conversation and an offer of living water?
Does being slow to judge mean pretending nothing matters? What did the Savior do with truth in this story?
What is the difference between looking at someone's past and looking at their possible?

segments.name: Judging eyes or helping hands
steps: Hand each team one slip. Situations: a new person walks into a youth activity knowing no one; a friend who stopped coming to church shows up again; someone's embarrassing mistake is being passed around a group chat; a classmate with a rough reputation asks to join your table.
Give teams three minutes to plan a 30-second scene that shows only the helping-hands response: what you would say and do in the first minute.
Have each team act its scene. After each, ask the watchers the first question below.
Read President Farnes's words from the aligned quotes. Tell them Elder Sinclair prayed that people who meet us would know they have “come home.”
questions: What exactly did they do that would make that person feel safe?
Which of these four is hardest for you in real life, and why?

segments.name: Pick your person
steps: Read the invitation from the talk (T33.12). Point out that Elder Sinclair named friends and new members in particular.
Read the fourth key quote (T33.13). Explain that he testified our small, one-by-one help is part of preparing the world for the Savior's return.
Give two silent minutes. In a phone note or on paper, each youth writes one name and one thing they will do for that person by Wednesday. Nobody has to show it.
Quick check: go around the room and have each person finish in five words or fewer: Quick to help looks like...
Tell them you will ask next week for one-sentence reports, with no names. Testify that the Savior treats each of them the way He treated the woman at the well.

key_quotes.text: But instead of being aggravated, she wanted to help.
a true disciple of Jesus Christ is quick to help and slow to judge
He spoke to the woman with dignity, not shame. He earnestly listened to her questions and responded with teaching, not ridicule. He did not hold her hostage to her history. He trusted her with truth.
when we help people, one by one, in our own small and simple ways, rather than judge them, we are preparing the world for the Second Coming of Jesus Christ

scriptures.use: Teams race to list every action of the Savior that helped the woman at the well, then compare the list with Elder Sinclair's description.
Challenge youth to read it on their own this week and text one thought to a parent or leader.
Read aloud just before the silent writing; ask how people will be able to tell whose disciples we are.

aligned_quotes.speaker: President Farnes
aligned_quotes.text: Let us put compassion into action and minister to the person in front of us.

aligned_quotes.speaker: President Chibota
aligned_quotes.text: He sees not only who we are but who we can become.

invitations.text: we are invited to reorient our souls so we may help friends and new members in more Christlike ways

takeaways: A true disciple of Jesus Christ is quick to help and slow to judge.
The Savior spoke to the woman at the well with dignity and trusted her with truth.
I can look at a person's possible, not only at their past.
act: By Wednesday, do the one thing you wrote down for the person you chose.
The next time a group chat or conversation turns to mocking someone, say something kind about that person or change the subject.
At your next class or activity, be the first to talk to someone who is new or sitting alone.
Read John 4:4–42 and mark every place the Savior helps.
adapt: At home or with two or three youth: do the well race as one team against the clock, and talk through two of the situations without acting them.
Large class: run the scenes in two halves of the room at once and have each half choose one scene to show everyone.
Short on time: do the one-arm challenge, the buttons story, the third key quote with its questions, and the silent writing.

children.title: Quick Helping Hands
children.big_idea: Jesus is kind and quick to help, and I can be quick to help too.
children.objective: Children will say that Jesus helps people kindly and will choose one way to use their helping hands this week.
prepare: Read Elder Sinclair's story of James and the buttons (the first part of his talk).
Bring a jacket, sweater or shirt with a button, if you have one.
Bring a clear cup of water for showing only, not for drinking.
Bring paper and crayons for each child.
Practice the saying with actions: Quick to help (hands reach out fast), slow to judge (shake head slowly, then stop and smile).

segments.name: Sing and say
steps: After the prayer, sing one verse of I'm Trying to Be like Jesus.

Teach the saying with its actions: Quick to help, slow to judge. Explain slow to judge in simple words: when someone makes a mistake, I do not get grumpy or decide they are bad. I look for a way to help.
Say it together three times: soft, medium, then strong.

segments.name: James and the buttons
steps: Show the button on the jacket. Tell the children that Elder Sinclair told a story in general conference about a boy named James in a Primary program.

Tell it simply: James had a new suit. He buttoned his sleeve to the front of his jacket, and his arm got stuck. Invite everyone to hold a wrist against the opposite shoulder and try to wiggle free without letting go.
Say that a grown-up watching felt grumpy. Have the children make a grumpy face and shake their heads. Ask: Did that help James? Let them answer no.
Say that a little girl sitting by James reached up with her fingers and undid the button. On the count of three, everyone says pop and lets their arm go free.
Tell them the grown-up was Elder Sinclair, and he said the little girl taught him to be more like Jesus.
questions: How do you think James felt when his arm was stuck?
How do you think he felt when the girl helped him?

segments.name: Helping hands game
steps: Have the children stand. Tell them that when you describe someone who needs help, they stretch out their hands fast and say, Quick to help.

Call out simple pretend situations one at a time: someone dropped their crayons; a new child does not know where to sit; a little one cannot zip a coat; someone spilled water; a friend made a mistake in a game.
After each one, choose a child to say or show what their helping hands could do.
Finish with the full saying and actions once more.

segments.name: Jesus at the well
steps: Have the children sit. Hold up the cup of water. Ask where people got water long ago, and explain what a well is.
Tell the story from John 4 simply: Jesus was tired from walking and sat by a well. A woman came by herself to get water. Jesus asked her for a drink.

Say that Jesus was kind to her. He listened to her questions and taught her. He told her He could give her “living water.” Elder Sinclair said Jesus offered her grace and help that could change her life.
Tell them she was so glad that she hurried to tell other people about Jesus.
Ask the questions, then repeat together: Jesus is quick to help.
questions: How did Jesus treat the woman at the well?
How does Jesus help you?

segments.name: Draw my helping hand
steps: Give each child paper and a crayon. Help them trace one hand.
Inside the hand, each child draws one way to help someone quickly this week at home, at church or at school.
Walk around and ask each child to tell you about the drawing. Write a few words on it for those who want help.
Let two or three children show their hands to the group.

segments.name: Promise and testify
steps: Tell the children that Elder Sinclair said a true disciple of Jesus Christ is quick to help and slow to judge. A disciple is someone who follows Jesus.
Check understanding: ask, What can you do when someone makes a mistake or gets stuck? Let several children answer, then do the saying with actions one last time.
Invite each child to take the paper hand home, put it where they will see it, and do what they drew.
Tell them that next week you will ask who used their helping hands. Bear a short testimony that Jesus loves them and helps them, and that they are like Him when they help.

key_quotes.text: But instead of being aggravated, she wanted to help.
a true disciple of Jesus Christ is quick to help and slow to judge
“And a little child shall lead them.”

scriptures.use: Read or tell it as you hold up the cup of water: Jesus asked the woman at the well for a drink and was kind to her.
Elder Sinclair began with the last phrase of this verse. Tell the children that they can show grown-ups how to help, just as the little girl did.
Older children read it aloud at the end; ask how people will know we follow Jesus.

aligned_quotes.speaker: President Farnes
aligned_quotes.text: Let us put compassion into action and minister to the person in front of us.

takeaways: Jesus is kind and quick to help.
I can be quick to help and slow to judge.
When I help someone, I am following Jesus.
act: Do the helping act you drew inside your paper hand.
When someone makes a mistake this week, ask, Can I help you?
Say hello to a child at church or school who is new or alone.
music: I'm Trying to Be like Jesus

adapt.younger: Ages 3–7: keep the stories to a few sentences each and act them twice. Use only three situations in the game. Let a helper trace hands. Shorten the saying to Quick to help and repeat it often with the reaching action. Sing Kindness Begins with Me if the children need to move again.
adapt.older: Ages 8–11: have a child read John 4:7 and another read John 13:34–35 aloud. Ask the harder question: Why is it sometimes easier to be grumpy with someone than to help? Let an older child lead the helping hands game by making up the situations, and have them write a sentence in the paper hand as well as draw.
